frameworks.name: Scaling Success Framework
frameworks.definition: Three load-bearing variables for business success: products customers love and repurchase, pricing that generates significant gross profits, and reinvestment velocity to achieve disproportionate growth.

claims.text: Success does not require going through hell; it requires learning the skills needed to achieve material business success. Learning these skills is often painful because mistakes hurt when you do not yet possess the competencies, but the pain is incidental to learning, not a prerequisite.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to inherited wealth or dynastic transmission (founder has wealthy parent who can teach shortcuts)

claims.text: A founder with a wealthy mentor (e.g., a Rockefeller parent) could acquire key business competencies with significantly less personal suffering than self-taught founders, because the mentor directly transmits knowledge rather than the student learning through trial-and-error.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has access to wealthy knowledgeable mentor
claims.mechanism: Direct knowledge transmission replaces costly trial-and-error learning

claims.text: Suffering is a universal fact of life across all income levels; both poor and wealthy people experience pain. The framing that success requires suffering is survivorship bias—people ask successful founders 'did a hard childhood cause your success?' while not asking this of unsuccessful people who also had hard childhoods.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Survivorship bias in retrospective causation: when comparing only successful individuals, unobserved confounders (hard work, luck, timing, product fit) are attributed to visible co-factors (hardship) that also appear in unsuccessful populations.
bounded_by: Assumes comparable sample sizes of successful and unsuccessful people with hard childhoods

claims.text: The few behaviors that appear across all successful business builders are: (1) behaviors that promoted activities; (2) activities that promoted products; (3) products that customers loved enough to repurchase; (4) pricing at points that generated significant gross profits; (5) reinvestment of profits into the business to achieve disproportionate growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: portfolio of ~60 businesses tracked by Acquisition.com

numbers.axis: common variables across successful business outcomes

anchors.value: all successful businesses demonstrate 5 load-bearing variables
suffering level varies widely; only the 5 variables are invariant

bounded_by: Does not include ventures with no repeat customers or negative unit economics

claims.text: The personal characteristics of the founder (e.g., hardship experienced, intrinsic drive source, educational background) are not load-bearing variables for business success; the business mechanics (customer love, pricing, reinvestment) are deterministic across all founders regardless of origin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: material business success is the outcome measure
bounded_by: Does not apply to ventures where founder brand/credibility is the primary product (personal coaching, celebrity endorsement)

claims.text: Successful people in retrospect assign causation to hardship (e.g., 'my hard childhood made me successful') by retracing data after the outcome is known, not by prospective prediction. The same hardships appear in unsuccessful populations, making the attribution unfalsifiable without randomized comparison.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Post-hoc rationalization: once an outcome is known, human cognition selects confirming antecedents and ignores the base rate of similar antecedents in failure cases.

examples.text: If a founder's father were Rockefeller (wealthy, knowledgeable), and the founder had ambition, the father could teach the son many business skills that would otherwise require painful learning-by-mistakes in the market. This example illustrates the claim that suffering is learnable-cost dependent, not success-dependent.

When successful entrepreneurs are asked 'Did your hard childhood make you successful?', the question carries implicit survivor bias: unsuccessful people also experienced hard childhoods, but their hard childhoods did not produce success. This reveals that hardship is neither necessary nor sufficient for business success.

practices.text: For business owners not growing as fast as desired: identify which stage of the 10-stage scaling roadmap your business occupies (product-market fit stage, early growth stage, mid-market stage, etc.). Use the Acquisition.com portfolio analysis to understand what other businesses struggled with at your stage and how they solved it.

When evaluating why a business succeeded or failed, focus first on the five load-bearing variables (do customers repurchase, is gross margin sufficient, did profits get reinvested) before attributing causation to founder characteristics or origin stories.
